ai-at-work.title: Anthropic gets its first court win over the Pentagon’s supply chain risk label
ai-at-work.excerpt: A federal judge ruled the Trump administration illegally labeled Anthropic a supply chain risk, handing the AI company a victory as its second Pentagon lawsuit continues in Washington.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic won a court challenge against the Trump administration's decision to label it a supply chain risk for Pentagon contracting purposes. This matters because it sets precedent for how government can classify AI companies and affects which vendors can participate in federal contracts, something digital workplace leaders need to watch if their organizations depend on emerging AI tools. Here's the thing: when courts start second-guessing supply chain risk labels, it means those labels need to actually mean something beyond political theater, which is probably good for everyone who takes security seriously.

ai-at-work.title: Anthropic and OpenAI are joining the AI stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
ai-at-work.excerpt: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, the AI Stage is back to dig into the single hottest topic in the community for the past few years, presented by Google for Startups.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic and OpenAI are both speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026's AI Stage, which Google for Startups is sponsoring. This matters because these two companies are shaping how AI gets integrated into workplace tools, and their public messaging directly influences what your organization will be asked to adopt in the next 18 months. My take: when both competitors show up at the same event to talk AI, you can bet the real news isn't what they say on stage, it's what gets announced in the hallway conversations afterward.

ai-at-work.title: Barret Zoph, the Thinking Machines co-founder ousted before joining OpenAI, is now at Google
ai-at-work.excerpt: Zoph, who co-founded Thinking Machines Lab alongside Mira Murati and also served as the startup's CTO, led a brief stint at OpenAI and is now at Google.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Barret Zoph, who co-founded Thinking Machines Lab and briefly worked at OpenAI, has landed at Google in what appears to be another career pivot in the AI space. This matters because top talent movement between OpenAI, Google, and other AI shops signals where the real innovation pressure points are and which companies are winning the war for AI expertise. The guy's résumé reads like he's playing musical chairs with every hot AI company in Silicon Valley, which honestly tells you more about AI leadership instability than it does about his actual capabilities.

ai-at-work.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and 100 other companies call for action to defend against rogue AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: Some of the world's largest tech companies and AI startups have come together to decry the current state of cybersecurity and to advertise a new solution that they say can ward off a new generation of
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A bunch of AI companies including OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic are basically saying "hey, we built powerful tools and now we're worried about bad actors using them, so here's our fix." This matters because if AI gets weaponized at scale, your digital workplace infrastructure becomes a target whether you work in AI or not. My take: it's a bit rich hearing from the companies that just spent years moving fast and breaking things, now asking everyone to slow down and think about security, but I'll take the wake-up call.

tools-tech.title: Even an AI cost-management vendor can lose control of its agent spending
tools-tech.excerpt: In one instance, an AI agent stayed open for four days and ran 4,819 calls for almost $4,000. No one had budgeted for this cost.
tools-tech.dwp_take: An AI cost-management vendor lost control of its own agent spending when a system ran nearly 5,000 calls over four days with zero budget oversight, racking up four grand in unexpected costs. This matters because it shows that even companies selling cost controls don't have their own houses in order, which should make any enterprise skeptical about trusting these tools with mission-critical spending. The real lesson here is that AI agents need guardrails like actual humans do, except nobody seems to want to build them until after they've burned through the quarterly budget.

tools-tech.title: Why AI doesn’t make companies more productive
tools-tech.excerpt: In 1987, Nobel Prize–winning economist Robert Solow wrote, “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” The same could be said about AI today. Gartner projects worldwi
tools-tech.dwp_take: A new study highlights what economists have known for decades: throwing money at technology doesn't automatically make work faster or better, and AI spending is exploding while actual productivity gains remain mysteriously absent. This matters to digital workplace folks because you're probably getting pressure to deploy AI everywhere when the real work is figuring out which problems AI actually solves versus which ones just need better processes or training. After 30 years, I can tell you the pattern never changes: new tech arrives, companies overspend on it, then wonder why Karen in accounting still can't find the file she needs.

tools-tech.title: UK says ‘no’ to backdoors, but the government isn’t listening
tools-tech.excerpt: It doesn’t matter what the UK government says, the majority of the UK public is reluctant to hand over additional surveillance powers that require tech companies to build backdoors to access encrypted
tools-tech.dwp_take: The UK public strongly opposes government demands for encryption backdoors, according to a CDT poll, yet UK officials continue pushing for access to encrypted communications anyway. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because your organization's security posture sits squarely in the crosshairs of this policy battle. It's the classic Washington move: ignore what voters actually want and do it anyway, except this time it's happening in Westminster, and your data security is the collateral damage.

tools-tech.title: If OpenAI has nothing to hide, it has nothing to fear
tools-tech.excerpt: Apple has filed a motion demanding expedited discovery in its trade secrets litigation against OpenAI. The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI and some former Apple employees now at the AI firm deliberately w
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple is suing OpenAI over alleged theft of trade secrets by former Apple employees now working at the AI company, and Apple wants the court to speed up the discovery process to prove it. This matters because if there's any substance to these claims, it highlights a real risk digital workplace leaders need to think about: how easily sensitive information can walk out the door when skilled people move between competing companies. Look, the headline tries to sound noble, but in reality both companies have plenty to hide and plenty of lawyers ready to hide it, so let's skip the moral theater here.

digital-culture.title: What to do if your coworker is lying
digital-culture.excerpt: Think a coworker is lying to you? Here are three tips from a veteran detective on how to handle it.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece on spotting and handling dishonesty in the workplace, pulling advice from an experienced detective on reading people and situations. This matters because digital workplaces often make deception easier (easier to hide behind text, harder to read body language), so knowing how to handle it protects team trust and productivity. Here's the thing though: most workplace lies are small, dumb ones born from fear or laziness, not Sherlock Holmes material, so sometimes the real move is just asking the person directly instead of playing detective.

digital-culture.title: Hiring program in energy tech sector enlists military veterans to fill data center skills gap
digital-culture.excerpt: With an unprecedented surge in demand for skilled technicians, Schneider Electric eyes talent with military experience.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Schneider Electric is deliberately recruiting military veterans to fill data center technician roles as demand for skilled workers outpaces supply in the energy tech sector. This matters because it highlights how traditional talent pipelines have dried up, forcing companies to look beyond conventional recruiting and recognize that military training translates directly to complex technical work. Smart move, honestly. Veterans bring discipline, systems thinking, and the ability to work under pressure without needing someone to explain why protocols exist.

digital-culture.title: Inside Meta’s Push to Put Robots to Work in Data Centers
digital-culture.excerpt: The company is testing robots that can swap cables, reset servers, and take on other tasks performed by technicians, fueling concerns among some workers that their jobs could be at risk.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Meta is deploying robots in its data centers to handle physical tasks like cable swapping and server resets that human technicians currently do. This matters because data center infrastructure underpins every digital workplace, so automation here eventually affects how workplace tech gets built, scaled, and maintained. Look, robots are fine at repetitive physical work, but the real question is whether Meta will reinvest those savings into better systems for the rest of us or just pocket the efficiency gains and call it innovation.

digital-culture.title: AI Agents Are Hacking Systems. Could That Push the US and China to Cooperate?
digital-culture.excerpt: This week on “Uncanny Valley,” senior writer Will Knight talks his recent visit to China and the future of AI collaboration.
digital-culture.dwp_take: An article explores whether AI security threats might actually push the US and China toward cooperation on AI safety standards and threat mitigation. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because AI security vulnerabilities directly impact enterprise systems, employee data, and the tools we're rapidly integrating into daily workflows. Here's the thing though: relying on geopolitical crises to force tech companies into security standards is exactly backwards, and we'll probably keep getting hacked in the meantime while bureaucrats figure out how to play nice.

industry-news.title: ARIA Bans Fully AI-Generated Songs From Australian Music Charts
industry-news.excerpt: ARIA now requires Australian chart-eligible music to be substantially human-made, excluding songs where AI creates the primary creative elements. The post ARIA Bans Fully AI-Generated Songs From Austr
industry-news.dwp_take: Australia's music chart authority decided that AI-generated songs need at least some human fingerprints on them to chart, meaning the algorithm can help but can't run the whole show. This matters to digital workplace folks because it signals how regulatory bodies worldwide are drawing lines around AI's creative role, which directly affects content teams and creative departments scrambling to figure out what's actually allowed. Honestly, it's refreshing to see someone say "nice try, robot" instead of just accepting every algorithm's output as legitimate art.

industry-news.title: Cyberattack on 3 UK Airports Exposes Data of 8.7 Million Customers
industry-news.excerpt: A cyberattack on Manchester Airports Group exposed information belonging to about 8.7 million customers across three UK airports. The post Cyberattack on 3 UK Airports Exposes Data of 8.7 Million Cust
industry-news.dwp_take: Hackers broke into Manchester Airports Group systems and compromised personal data for 8.7 million passengers across three UK airports. This matters because airport operations run on integrated digital systems, and when those get breached, it exposes the ripple effect of poor security across interconnected workplace infrastructure that handles sensitive customer information. Here's the thing: if airports can't lock down their own networks, how are they supposed to secure the traveler data flowing through them, and more importantly, what does that say about the digital workplace security posture of critical infrastructure in general?

industry-news.title: Claude Memory Now Follows You Into Cowork — Here’s How to Turn It Off
industry-news.excerpt: Claude now shares memory across Chat and Cowork. Here’s how to pause, reset, or limit what Claude remembers and what controls users still lack. The post Claude Memory Now Follows You Into Cowork — Her
industry-news.dwp_take: Anthropic expanded Claude's memory feature so conversations persist across both the Chat and Cowork products, meaning your AI assistant now remembers things you told it in one place when you use the other. For teams relying on Claude for collaboration work, this creates consistency but also raises questions about data isolation and whether sensitive project details should be floating around in an AI's memory bank. My take: it's useful until someone complains that Claude remembered their "confidential" strategy discussion from last Tuesday, then suddenly everyone wants the nuclear option.

industry-news.title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 Camera Setup Shows How Samsung Reworked the Fold
industry-news.excerpt: The Galaxy Z Fold 8’s redesigned shape changes how its cameras fit into daily use, while the Ultra offers stronger optical zoom. The post Galaxy Z Fold 8 Camera Setup Shows How Samsung Reworked the Fo
industry-news.dwp_take: Samsung redesigned the Galaxy Z Fold 8's physical shape to better accommodate its camera system, with the Ultra model getting beefier optical zoom capabilities. This matters because foldables are finally becoming realistic daily drivers for knowledge workers who need decent imaging on the go, not just novelty devices. After three decades watching mobile tech, I can tell you it's refreshing when manufacturers actually solve problems instead of just adding features and calling it innovation.
